style: former options HFT / market-structure whistleblower
markets: US options, US equities (hedging)
edge_principles: Speed alone is not an edge; it only matters when racing others to the same stale quote. A durable edge needs something more (e.g. modelling implied-vol supply/demand).
In options market making, risk management means finding the cheapest effective hedge for existing inventory; poor hedging leaks alpha via slippage and adverse selection.
Fees can turn a gross-profitable high-turnover book unprofitable; model fees per venue.
When fills on certain venues turn toxic, route away and investigate exchange order-type changes.
Retail market orders are mostly internalized by wholesalers; active traders should use low-commission direct-routing brokers and watch fill rates on resting orders.
notes: Market-structure episode (HFT order types, payment for order flow). No concrete setup; relevant to MCF only as cost and fill-quality awareness.

style: host progress update; retail swing trader learning Python, VWAP-focused intraday coach
markets: US stocks, some futures
edge_principles: Time stop: if an intraday trade has not moved into profit within roughly 10 candles or ~30 one-minute bars, exit; good trades tend to work almost immediately.
Define the exit plan (scalp target vs hold-to-close vs multi-day swing) before entry, not after the trade is moving.
Do not chase a few cents of better entry or wait for a few cents above breakeven on the exit; the first and last ticks are the most expensive.
Structure scans in three layers: universals (price, average volume, listing), conditions (above VWAP, RSI band, relative volume) and triggers (the exact event that fires the entry).
Relative volume (today's volume vs. the 20-day average at the same time) shows where participation is surging; standard-deviation band width or ATR measures available opportunity.
Use a basket of uncorrelated strategies across timeframes to smooth the equity curve; no single system fits all regimes.
Monte Carlo resampling of the trade list shows the range of drawdown paths for the same edge.
Multi-day (anchored, 2-5 day) VWAP marks where larger funds are averaging into multi-day orders; VWAP works best on liquid, algorithm-heavy large caps.
Make systematic mistakes rather than discretionary ones, so they can be measured and fixed; a loss within the plan is not a mistake.
Review journals weekly rather than obsessing daily; tag trades with market type, time of day and a confidence score.
notes: Conversational Q&A on progress, journaling, mentoring and VWAP philosophy. No complete setup; useful scan-structure and time-stop ideas.

style: retail discretionary intraday stock trader, flat overnight, order-book (Level 2) reader
markets: Australian equities (ASX)
edge_principles: Go home flat so the next morning can be spent on offense with fresh news names, not managing yesterday's positions.
Trade stocks with a catalyst (company news, broker rating changes, big commodity moves); the move per trade is large relative to commissions.
Avoid sleepy large caps without news; they chew up commissions and offer no edge.
Most profit comes in the first hour; be very selective midday when the market is not trending, and become active again in the last hour.
If a trade does not go in your favour straight away it is probably not a winner; exit quickly.
Size positions to the visible liquidity you could exit into near your stop; do not take more shares than the bids behind you can absorb.
As size grows, move from pure order-book scalps to momentum/trend trades in strong stocks, where liquidity is deeper than the book shows.
Keep commissions low (negotiate per-trade costs, avoid minimum ticket charges); costs decide whether short-term trading is viable.
notes: Australian intraday trader whose edge is catalyst selection plus order-book timing. Two MCF-relevant ideas: catalyst gappers in the first 10-15 minutes and a market-day-filtered 52-week-high momentum breakout after 15 minutes.

style: quant fund (QTS Capital), intraday holds of several hours, multi-strategy
markets: FX, futures, US stocks (market-neutral), some options
edge_principles: Hold intraday for hours: enough trades for statistical significance (high Sharpe) without HFT infrastructure costs.
Mean-reversion strategies win often with occasional large losses (~10x a typical win); momentum strategies lose often with rare large wins. Judge each by its own profile.
No reliable regime switch was found to predict whether momentum or mean reversion will work next month; run both at once and diversify instead of timing.
Start a new strategy at very low leverage and scale up only as live results confirm it; never size from the backtest Sharpe. Allocation to strategies is the main discretionary decision.
Cut leverage on strategies whose live performance decays; keep a strategy pool where some die and some are born.

Treat a backtest as a test to reject a strategy, not proof. A high-Sharpe backtest lets you detect overfitting quickly in live trading (e.g. a three-week drawdown when the backtest says nearly every week is positive).
Data-snooping is the main backtest pitfall; keep models simple and economically sensible.
Model the bid-ask spread with quote data, and check that edge survives beyond top-of-book size; many high-frequency academic results vanish at 1,000+ shares.
Treat published strategies (books, papers) as inspiration and modify them; authors withhold details.
Override models around exceptional events (natural disasters, major economic events) by standing aside, since the model has no news input.
Fix a failing strategy with a targeted, re-backtested change; a change that lowers risk without raising return is still an improvement.
notes: Quant process episode: diversification, allocation, backtest hygiene. Only one concrete rule example (Bollinger mean reversion with a minimum band width).

style: retail short-term crypto trader (formerly penny stocks and options)
markets: Bitcoin (BTC/USD on offshore exchanges)
edge_principles: Blew up accounts by sizing too large and raising size after losing streaks (revenge trading); risk management is what turned results around.
Trader amnesia: start each day without carrying over the previous day's P&L emotions.
Do not chase a fixed daily dollar goal; P&L is non-linear and a few weeks make the year, so watching the P&L instead of the plan causes forced trades.
Treat news narratives as after-the-fact stories; repeated, known events (e.g. scheduled government coin auctions) get priced in.
In a market traded on several exchanges, watch the leading venues; a move on a leading exchange can be traded on a lagging one before prices converge.
Counterparty (exchange) risk is real and uninsured; keep it in sizing and capital allocation.
Flatten before sleeping even in a 24/7 market; average hold 4-8 hours.
notes: Crypto episode, mostly Bitcoin background. One loosely specified setup (Bollinger-band range-expansion breakout targeting prior order-block zones); not testable with MCF stock data.

style: fund of funds allocating to short-term quant strategies (T2AM); author of Inside the Black Box
markets: multi-asset systematic strategies; US equities market structure
edge_principles: Alpha is skill at timing the selection and sizing of holdings; being right too early is the same as being wrong.

A black box has five parts: alpha model (forecast), risk model (unwanted exposures), transaction cost model, portfolio construction (balance upside, risk and cost) and execution. All sit on research and clean data.
Codifying a strategy forces you to define universe, signal and price inputs precisely, which is where research adds value.
Model risk: a model simplifies the world, and unmodelled drivers (policy changes, events) can cause losses; humans spot these faster, machines execute more consistently.
A human override before sending trades (dropping names with unmodelled news) is a legitimate partial-systematic step.

Stale resting limit orders get picked off: TradeWorx measured ~1.7 cents/share between being first and last in the queue, far more than HFT profit per share. Expect adverse selection on passive fills.
HFT aggregate profit in US equities fell from ~$7.2B (2009) to ~$1B (2013), about $0.001/share; liquidity is cheap and markets are fairer than ever for retail.
notes: Quant structure and HFT market-structure episode. Only concrete trade idea is the fast-alpha pairs fade between two closely related stocks.

style: retail small-cap momentum day trader (Investors Underground), mainly short side
markets: US small-cap stocks
edge_principles: Trade only stocks with abnormal range and abnormal volume (millions of shares, well above normal); avoid thin names.
His journal showed all profits made from pre-market to 11:00, losses 11:00-12:00 and a little profit 15:00-16:00; concentrate activity in the morning.
Short squeezes on 30-40% runners often extend to 100%+; size small on big-range names because short losses are unbounded; easy borrow does not make a stock a good short.
Scale up by adding to winners only at a point where you would open a fresh position (pretend you are not in yet), not by doubling initial size.
Use a daily max loss (e.g. $500-1,000 for a ~$700/day trader); one uncapped losing day wipes out a month.
Aim for ~3:1 reward to risk and align goals with acceptable daily losses.
'Dale and bail, don't stay and pray': take the planned quick move and exit; staying to see what happens breaks accounts.
Watch crowd positioning: if everyone is short and price keeps rising, expect a squeeze; if everyone defends a falling long, wait for a washout.
Part-time traders should avoid volatile momentum names they cannot monitor and must use hard stops.
Keep a cash reserve so you never need to make money on a given day; wiring profits out was a crutch for sloppiness at larger size.
notes: Concrete small-cap momentum playbook: multi-day overextension short on the first crack, failed follow-through short at prior-day resistance, ABCD pullback long and morning washout long.

style: futures broker (Optimus Futures), observer of many retail traders
markets: futures (ES, 10-year notes, etc.)
edge_principles: Successful long-term traders use few variables and simple methods, each different from the next; risk management, not the method, is what they share.
Exit when the conditions that justified the entry are gone; price-based stops are better than purely dollar-based ones.
Experienced traders still feel the same discomfort as beginners; they follow the method over gut feel (e.g. adding into falling markets when the system says so).
Professional trading is mostly waiting; a day-trading method may only fire once a week.
Returns are lumpy; do not expect a steady monthly percentage or a fixed daily dollar target.
Choose the instrument by its daily range relative to your risk capital (e.g. 10-year notes move less than ES).
One-tick ES scalping is not realistic for retail latency and costs; demo results overstate live results.
Commissions matter in proportion to trade frequency; active traders should negotiate, while noting exchange and routing fees are fixed.
The main source of indiscipline is hoping to recover losses (adding to losers, 'just this time').
notes: Broker's view of trader traits, expectations and costs. No concrete setups.

style: retail part-time hybrid day/short-swing trader
markets: US stocks (biotech, sector rotation names); formerly OTC penny stocks
edge_principles: Made ~$500k in under 90 days on OTC marijuana stocks and lost it as fast by never taking profits and holding illiquid positions; take profits and respect liquidity.
Quitting a job too early adds income pressure that drives emotional trades; keep a job until finances are secure.
Scale in over 4-5 small entries rather than full size at once; the first entry is small so a wrong trade costs little.
Enter the hard stop immediately after the entry order so it cannot be moved; his worst losses came from moving stops on shorts and adding.
Hold overnight only on a strong close (near the high of the move); exit weak closes, especially in gappy markets.
Use larger timeframes (daily/weekly) for selection; 1-2 minute charts created noise and spooked him.
Review the trade log to find which setups actually produce profits and narrow to those.
Avoid crowded shorts; trade the less-crowded outliers in a hot sector.
notes: Part-time trader with clear swing management rules (scale out at +3% and +5%, strong-close hold rule) and two repeatable setups: range trading and shorting overextended sector-rotation outliers.

style: retail swing trader (2 days to 3 months) plus intraday open trading; Bulls on Wall Street
markets: US stocks
edge_principles: Trading = setups (one third), risk management (one third) and trade management (the decisive third, where fear and greed act).
'Set it and forget it': plan entry, stop and target before the trade (about 3:1) and avoid micromanaging on faster timeframes than the setup.
Pre-write entry range, stop range, target range and share size for each watchlist name so execution needs no thinking.
Keep a 10-15 setup toolkit and use what the current market rewards; setups stop working (breakouts fail in some markets, plain moving-average bounces get stop-hunted).
Place stops beyond where the crowd's obvious stops sit and allow for the stock's normal daily range; a 2-point stop on a stock with a 4-5 point daily range will get hit.
Top-down: market direction first, then weekly sector money-flow analysis, then a 50-150 name watchlist narrowed to 5-15 names per day.
Do not force long/short balance; lean with the market read (e.g. favour longs when deeply oversold).
Before going full time, hold enough capital that expenses never enter trading decisions (he suggests mid six figures, or double your estimate).
Set one learning goal per year and master it in stages: observe and log, then paper trade, then trade live.
notes: Swing trader whose main current setup is the moving-average 'remount' after a stop run, plus a rule for holding quality longs through macro-driven gap-downs.

style: prop futures trader and partner at Futex (London); ex-pit trader
markets: futures: Bund, Euro Stoxx; watches S&P, US 10-year, oil, FTSE
edge_principles: Work top-down: macro and central-bank context first, then support/resistance and trend lines, then volume profile/VWAP, then the price ladder for final confirmation.
In the short term fundamentals override technicals; know what the market is pricing (e.g. negative rates) before fading a move on a chart line.
Avoid 3-4 tick stops that algorithms shake out; anchor stops to structure.
Watch correlated markets (US 10-year for Bunds, oil for equities); the driver changes over time.
Early edges came from structural inefficiencies (cross-exchange Bund arbitrage, Bund/BTP spreads) that disappeared; edges decay, so keep adapting.
A team gives more eyes on the markets and catches setups an individual misses.
Rehearse event trading (ECB, payrolls) on recorded data replays to compress years of learning.
Expect sim consistency in about 5-6 months; live trading then becomes mostly a psychology problem; even at a prop firm fewer than half succeed.
When lost and frustrated, step away completely and seek trusted help rather than trading through it.
notes: Futures prop trader. Setups are price-ladder (order book) and volume-profile based, mostly beyond MCF's data except a volume-profile/value-area approximation.

style: NYSE floor broker ($2 commission broker) executing day-trading flow for a hedge fund
markets: US stocks, SPY, index futures; IPOs and secondaries
edge_principles: His remaining floor edge is in auction events: the opening print, IPOs and secondaries, and the closing auction, where order-imbalance information is visible.
Day trades held at most 2-3 hours; flat at the close apart from small reversal positions.
Rules for IPO and secondary trades come from historical data, and he follows them even against his own feel; probability beats opinion.
Known technical levels work because many participants act on them.
11:00 ET (European close) often brings a spike or sell-off in US stocks; the last 60-90 minutes of the US session usually moves and sets the tone globally.
Directional, high-volume days (index rebalances, option expiry, month/quarter end) are the busiest; Fed days can be choppy with confused closing flow.
Do not turn a reasonable profit into an unreasonable loss; avoid stubbornness.
notes: NYSE floor history and auction-based flow trading. Mostly needs imbalance data MCF lacks; one testable idea is the overnight reversal after extreme closes.

style: ex options market maker (Pacific Exchange, COMEX gold/silver), long-vol hedge fund, now runs a small quant group (TradeCo Global)
markets: options, futures (10-year notes, gold), stocks
edge_principles: Judge decisions by process, not outcome: a good decision can lose and a bad one can win; over many trades the law of large numbers rewards good process.
Positive expectation = P(win) x avg win - P(loss) x avg loss; bet small and many times like a casino, never risk ending the game.
Start research from precise, answerable questions from live observation (bottom up), then verify with data; anecdotal observations are often behavioural bias.
Combine top-down research ideas with bottom-up execution feedback; neither works alone.
Automate where markets are liquid and the human adds little at execution; keep human judgement for binary events (FDA, earnings, mergers).
'Rule of half': when a position feels wrong or uncomfortable, cut half to regain clear thinking, then reassess (possibly re-add).
Time-based exits are fine when the research behind the trade is time-based.
'One in a thousand year' moves happen about yearly in finance; your own large position changes the odds of loss.
Retail traders often assume an edge without verifying it; professionals specialise narrowly, seek arbitrage-like simple edges, and trade modest size.
Keep situational awareness: notice things that do not make sense (e.g. disputes over marks preceded the Bayou fund fraud).
notes: Probability and process episode. Concrete ideas are illustrative: a payroll-release first-move fade (offered as an example research question) and historical earnings-straddle pricing.

style: independent intraday technical crude-oil futures trader with fundamental overlay; ex-CBOT trade desk and prop
markets: crude oil futures (WTI), some swing positions
edge_principles: Repeat the same high-probability trades every day so the decision is mechanical; tight stop, move on if it fails.
3-5 day trades maximum; most of the day is waiting. 60 trades a day is overtrading and only pays the broker.
Know the fundamentals (supply shocks, OPEC headlines, refinery maintenance, EIA/IEA data) to understand why the market reacts, even if entries are technical.
Avoid thin sessions (Asia) where one 50-lot can move price; the European session is a calmer place for new traders to start; use the mini contract when learning.
Trade at most two markets; specialise in one you are passionate about.
Keep separate accounts for swing positions and day trades so you can day trade against the swing position and track each cleanly.
A prop firm forces discipline for new traders because someone monitors every trade.
notes: Crude-oil specialist using rotation levels, Fibonacci, volume profile/TPO and footprint. One loosely specified profile setup (single-print fills) and a seasonal crude view.

style: professional systematic-entry swing trader (discretionary market selection), part of a two-person team
markets: 36 futures and FX markets: stock indexes, bonds, metals, oil, majors FX, grains; UK stocks
edge_principles: Preserve 'mental capital': time entries so you are not offside for days; cut trades that are not working instead of waiting.
Enter as close to the session open as possible when momentum is highest; no new London-session trades after about 10:30, wait for the US open instead.
Discretion only in what to trade; entries, stops, stop moves and exits are rule-based.
Total open risk capped at 3% of the account; with several similar setups, choose the best or split the risk.
Select trades top-down on monthly, weekly then daily charts; use lower timeframes only for entry, never for flicking through looking for trades.
Avoid scheduled news events; weigh positioning and sentiment over fundamentals (if everyone is long, look to sell).
Reward rule-following, not P&L: treat yourself after a losing day where you followed every rule; not after a winning day where you broke rules.
Surviving the first year roughly flat without blowing up is a sign you can make it.
Compete only with yourself; cooperate with other traders; a mentor helped most with discipline, not setups.
notes: Swing trader using Fibonacci/harmonic confluence levels with moving-average entry triggers and close-based exits. One concrete setup.

style: 100% systematic trend-following, momentum and mean-reversion equity trader (The Chartist)
markets: Australian and US stocks (S&P 500, ASX 500, Russell 2000); index futures only to hedge
edge_principles: Know why a strategy makes money (cut losers and let winners run; stretched rubber band snaps back); a list of indicator conditions is not a reason.
Robustness: the same rules and parameters should work across many stocks and markets (S&P 500, ASX 500, Russell 2000) with no per-symbol optimisation.
Test on historical index constituents including delisted names to remove survivorship bias.
Trade frequency matters: more trades exploit the edge more often and give statistical confidence; be suspicious of < ~25 trades in 10 years, win rate > 75% or profit factor > 3.
Mean reversion adds diversification to trend following: higher win rate (60%+), faster drawdown recovery, 200-1000 trades a year.
Stress-test by trying to break the system: vary parameters +/-15-20%, randomise prices (e.g. opens), and Monte Carlo trade skipping when signals exceed capital.
Run the simulation side by side with live trading weekly; a slow divergence signals a problem (e.g. rising slippage of ~11%/yr killed an ASX momentum system).
A system out of sync with its regime is not broken (a long trend system will lose in sideways markets); a loss you cannot explain is the warning sign.
Follow the system on scary nights; skipping trades usually means missing the best ones.
Long only with a market-regime filter; shorting was dropped because of poor risk-adjusted returns and regulatory bans when it is needed most.
notes: Systems-robustness episode with concrete strategy families: oversold mean reversion with regime filter, cross-sectional momentum ranking, Bollinger breakout trend following, and a single-market GLD pattern he cites as non-robust.

style: trading psychologist and coach to hedge funds and prop market makers; part-time quantitative trader
markets: general (futures market makers, hedge fund PMs)
edge_principles: Separate logical from psychological problems: cutting winners early may just be failure to adapt targets to a lower volatility regime (e.g. VIX ~14 vs. 20s), where short-term moves mean-revert.
Scale profit targets and holding expectations to current volatility; in low-volatility regimes intraday moves revert more and trends scratch.
When a disciplined method starts losing, treat the losses as information that the market (volatility, trend, correlation, participants) has changed.
ABCD: Adapt to changing markets, Build on distinctive strengths, Cultivate creativity (a distinctive edge, not a book strategy), Develop best practices into processes.
Break a bad habit by noticing it as it starts (e.g. frustration before revenge trading), then step away and redirect.
Turn best practices into habits by repeating them daily (~30 days), not by motivational reminders.
Pick a holding period that fits your cognitive style; fast pattern-recognition scalping overloads some people who do well with intraday or overnight swings.
Avoid P&L-amount goals (they create performance anxiety); track improvement in risk-adjusted return (return per unit of risk) and think in basis points, not dollars.
Rehearse hitting stops with guided imagery so stop-outs feel routine.
Have something in life more important than trading so drawdowns do not break you; find fulfilment in markets, not only in profits.
notes: Psychology episode. No setups; the most MCF-relevant idea is adapting targets and holds to the volatility regime.

style: independent intraday/short-swing stock trader, ex-prop; high-beta names
markets: US stocks (FANG and other high-beta names: TSLA, NFLX, AMZN, GOOGL, PCLN, BIDU), some low-priced breakouts
edge_principles: Avoid trading off 1-minute charts where the crowd of under-funded traders gets stopped out; 60-minute candles remove noise (only six decisions per day).
Know where every moving average, Bollinger band and regression line sits before entry: price tends to stop at these supply/demand zones, so only take trades with enough room to the next zone.
Judge a high-beta stock against the index futures: making lower lows while futures rally signals a seller; do not buy it just because it ticked a prior candle high.
You do not need to win the day, only one of the hourly intervals; most stocks are untradable most of the time.
New traders should avoid the pre-market top-gainers list (low-float names up 90-200%); start with slower, orderly names.
Fixed max loss of 1% of account per trade; size = 1% / (entry - prior close); entries close to the prior close allow bigger size with the same dollar risk.
Take partial profit ('cash flow'), hold a runner with a break-even stop.
Review the month's results; ensure losing days stay in the normal range and never turn a paper cut into a large loss.
Prop trading as he knew it is mostly gone; if trading volume, negotiate commissions aggressively; avoid offshore 'brokers' that act as bookies.
Re-examine charts when nothing works for several days; markets keep changing and edges must be rediscovered.
notes: Two concrete setups: the 'PS60' hourly-candle pivot confirmation on high-beta stocks with room to the next MA/band level, and a daily range breakout from a nightly scan with a fixed-1% risk sizing rule.

style: CTA (Chesapeake Capital), original Turtle, long-term systematic trend follower
markets: ~120 futures markets plus ~100 single-stock futures/stocks; long and short
edge_principles: Turtle teachings: buy highs, sell lows, add to winners, never add to losers, trade small; good systems are uncomfortable and infrequently profitable.
Win rate low 40s; average win 2-3x average loss; 5-10% of trades make all the money. Do not tighten stops so much that the win rate falls into the 20s.
Sample size of the backtest is the most important statistic; simple systems (entry, exit, stop) give large samples, extra filters shrink them.
Use the same system and parameters for all markets, longs and shorts; per-market optimisation does not hold out of sample.
Trade a spread of parameters (e.g. 100 to 300-day lookbacks) rather than one 'best' setting; individual trades are random as to which parameter wins.
Markets got choppier as trend followers multiplied; the main change over 30 years was moving to longer holding periods (average about one year).
Include shorts: they add diversification even if their average trade is worse; long-only sector funds suffer in big down-trends.
Judge yourself by rule-following, not short-term performance; a disciplined average system beats an abandoned good one.
Set leverage you can live with at the start; if too large, cut once, then return to robotic execution; separate research, signal generation and execution where possible.
Diversification across sectors (keep ~25% risk in commodities) matters more as assets grow; pure volatility targeting by large CTAs can amplify sell-offs.
notes: Trend-following philosophy episode. Concrete rule family: multi-lookback moving-average/breakout trend following across all markets, long and short, with long holds.

style: retired value-oriented long/short hedge fund manager (IT/telecom specialist)
markets: Nordic and global equities
edge_principles: Deep business understanding pays off mainly when something changes suddenly (acquisition, strategy shift); in normal times stocks trade in patterns where an analyst adds little.
Be patient: if you feel rushed you are probably late; opportunities cycle back. Individuals can wait, institutions often cannot.
Never go all in; keep dry powder, especially for adding in crashes.
Seek out the opposite view (sell-side cases, information that hurts) to counter confirmation bias.
Position limits: at most ~5% of fund in one stock and ~20-25% in one industry spread over several names.
Running with the crowd is usually right; keep independent judgment for the ~10% of times when you must diverge.
Value views can be wrong for years (he was too bearish 2012-2015); early successes may be luck that builds confidence.
notes: Value investing, career and AI/transhumanism discussion. No intraday or testable setups.

style: aggressive retail/educator options and index-futures swing trader (Simpler Trading)
markets: US stock options (TSLA, FB, AAPL, GLD), E-mini S&P/Nasdaq futures
edge_principles: Do not chase a move you missed; another opportunity comes, and emotional entries make you miss the real setups.
Flat is a position: when there is nothing to do, do nothing; one or two days a month offer the chance for an above-normal size trade.
Waiting for every indicator to confirm makes you the last buyer; overly fearful traders enter when they should be taking profits.
His blow-ups came from focusing on a big account target ($1M) and refusing to take losses to reach it.
Exits matter more than entries: take most of the position off at 'low-hanging fruit' targets (1.272 Fibonacci extension, or the options-implied expected move) and move the stop to break-even.
Sweet spot is 2 days to 2 weeks; very active day trading on small accounts can cost ~100% of the account per year in commissions.
Concentrate on a few strong positions rather than 18 small ones.
If a setup is not obvious within a second of looking at the chart, move on; looking longer means forcing a bias.
Use at most about three indicators; test a setup over 25 consecutive trades before judging it.
For options beginners: buy in-the-money options rather than cheap out-of-the-money ones; add put/call credit spreads; skip complex structures.
notes: Options/futures swing trader. Two concrete setups: the 'squeeze' (Bollinger bands inside Keltner channels) with Fibonacci-extension scale-outs, and a heavily-shorted-stock intraday reversal (TSLA example).

style: ex-prop (Bright Trading) day trader; statistics-driven intraday mean reversion in one product; co-developer of a tape-reading algorithm used by a hedge fund
markets: E-mini S&P 500 futures (formerly US stocks)
edge_principles: Index futures trend on only ~10-15% of days; on range days mean reversion has the edge, so build around range statistics.
Do not fade before at least 40% of the 14-day ATR has been traded (true on ~94% of days); fade near the level that a range-prediction model says covers ~80% of days.
Use statistical magnets as targets: VWAP (HFT activity tends to revert price to it), prior-day high or low (one is touched on ~88% of days), daily pivot (~70%).
Set stops outside noise: about 3x the average 1-minute bar range (6-8 ES points); a wide stop you will actually hold beats a tight one you will fiddle with.
Trade in two scales: first scale at ~3-4 points to relieve pressure, second at 7-9+; if price runs 3 points against you and returns to entry, cut half rather than fiddle.
Enter at full planned size at the level, no averaging; if price misses the level by two ticks, do not chase.
Trading fewer days is fine: he traded 13 of ~20 sessions in March; when markets are tight and nothing sets up, do nothing.
Specialise in one product or niche to know its statistics intimately; that confidence is what allows sizing up while the edge lasts.
As a one-person business, push size when you have a proven edge; illness or life events can stop you at any time.
Regime (range expansion vs contraction) determines which trades are active; a sputtering strategy after a strong run signals a regime change: reduce size rather than predict turns.
Trade-off of edges: the Russell rebalance closing trade worked for years and was then arbitraged away.
notes: Highly quantitative S&P futures day trader. Several concrete, testable mean-reversion rules with stated probabilities; directly translatable to SPY 5-min data.

style: market-data developer (Nanex), HFT critic; former 1980s algorithmic S&P futures trader
markets: US equities, options and futures market structure
edge_principles: Displayed liquidity across fragmented US exchanges is often not all fillable: fast firms cancel or trade ahead when they see your order execute elsewhere; expect partial fills on large market orders.

Mini flash crashes (hundreds of trades in under a second moving large caps several percent, then reversing) occur many times a day; resting stop orders get triggered by them, so prefer stop logic based on bar closes or time filters rather than raw stop orders.
Limit Up-Limit Down bands (about 5% from a rolling 5-minute reference) act as magnets for these micro crashes, which now often travel the full band before reversing.
Spreads measured as a 1-cent quote can hide 1% swings within a second; measure execution cost with realistic intrasecond data.
Consider avoiding the opening auction scramble; there is no standard order to buy at a set time after the open, so build it yourself (e.g. enter at 9:45).
He quit his own profitable trading because he kept second-guessing his system; software follows rules, people do not.
notes: Market-structure episode (Nanex, SIP latency, quote stuffing, mini flash crashes). No setups; relevant to MCF for stop-order handling and fill realism.

style: discretionary order-flow scalper ('low-frequency market maker') plus partner in a multi-market quant research firm
markets: US Treasury futures (10-year, 2-year), Eurodollar strips, commodity spreads (crack, metals); quant firm trades 20-50 futures markets
edge_principles: Retail traders over-focus on the entry ('method hunting'); edge mostly comes from the risk model: bet size, payout odds, volatility adaptation and trade count.
Like a casino, edge needs many occurrences; a single-market intraday strategy with few trades cannot rely on the risk model alone.
Know what your strategy is meant to be: high win rate (market making, inefficiency-based) or ~50% win rate with 2:1+ payoffs. Taking 1-point wins against 3-point stops inverts the risk math.

Automating his discretionary scalping failed because small discretionary adjustments (volatility adaptation, skipped trades, size tweaks) carried the edge; short-term single-market trading suits discretion, longer-term multi-market trading suits full automation.
A stop is a placeholder that defines risk per trade; convert it to percent of equity and size accordingly; changing trade frequency changes the risk model.
Diversify by strategy and holding period, not only by market (markets are often highly correlated).
Do not judge a model on a handful of trades; evaluate a day trader's results over at least a month of trades.
Mouse traders cannot compete with HFT top-of-book market makers on 50% win rate tick scalps; single-venue futures still allow discretionary order-flow scalping, fragmented equities much less so.
Interacting daily with other traders (journals, chats) noticeably improved his and members' trading; 'don't trade in a closet'.
Reported that average retail account attrition is under three months.
notes: Risk-model-centric episode. Concrete items: order-book scalping (not testable) and a non-predictive multi-market quant approach whose edge is claimed to come only from volatility-adaptive sizing and payout asymmetry.

style: non-trader CEO of an education business (Sang Lucci) and a trader-incubating hedge fund (mostly automated traders)
markets: US equities and futures (as allocator/operator)
edge_principles: The fund backs mostly automated traders: rule enforcement, testability and predictable execution made them more successful than discretionary traders in their experience.
Survive first ('keep your seat at the table'): no terminal risk, because many traders make most of a year's income in one or two trades.

Owning a strategy means knowing everything that could break it (macro regime, queue-priority rule changes), its max drawdown, Sharpe/Sortino and capital needs well beyond the worst drawdown, not just a six-month backtest.
Edges disappear; traders must keep reinventing their trades.
Learn by reverse-engineering the best trader's fills against the tape for hours after the close (how Sang Lucci learned tape reading).
Humility and a defensive mindset distinguish long-lived traders; the very rich ones carry themselves like normal people.

Physical state affects decisions: sleep, nutrition, exercise and meditation compound into better performance over a career; heart-rate variability could be used by risk managers to cut size on exhausted traders.
Understand the incentives of everyone who touches your order (introducing broker, executing broker, clearing firm, exchange) and negotiate commissions.
notes: Operator/psychology episode about evaluating traders and performance optimisation. No setups.

style: part-time retail trend/position trader (won City Index Trading Academy 2012)
markets: US stocks (long and short); earlier index spread bets
edge_principles: React, don't predict: take the signal, place the stop, let the system run; tinkering with stops caused his early problems.
Entry precision matters little for multi-month holds; market-on-open entries are fine.
Size each trade from the planned stop: 2-4% of account at risk, more for smooth trends, less for choppy charts.
Keep about eight concentrated positions, roughly balanced long/short and across sectors, to hedge general market moves.
Expect many small losses while a few big winners build; judge the portfolio, not single trades.
Treat losing trades like a parachutist's hundredth jump: routine.
Learn from successful traders' published methods (Livermore, Darvas, Turtles) and give them time; no need for income pressure from trading.
Trying to win each week in a competition (rather than just avoid elimination) and day trading were stressful; position trading fits a day job.
notes: Simple, fully specified Turtle-style 52-week breakout position system on US stocks with Donchian exits.

style: market-structure / trading-venue developer (ex-RBC electronic trading, THOR router)
markets: US equities market structure
edge_principles: Displayed size across exchanges often vanishes when you try to take it: fast traders see your fills on the nearest venue and cancel on the others; routing that times orders to arrive at all venues together (THOR) captured all displayed shares.
Large orders sent aggressively to exchanges create immediate impact; dark pools with minimum-quantity orders let size cross without impact at the cost of possible non-execution.
Maker-taker rebates create broker conflicts of interest (routing for rebates rather than fills); retail market orders mostly go to wholesalers via payment for order flow.
Stale quotes during price transitions are picked off by faster traders; IEX's ~350 microsecond speed bump prevents trades at stale prices.
For backtests and simulation, assume worse fills on large marketable orders than the displayed book suggests.
notes: Market-structure episode about IEX, speed bumps and dark pools. Mentions an opening-imbalance dislocation study (stocks with big open imbalances dislocate at the open and come back) but gives no tested rule. No setups recorded.

style: ex-LIFFE runner, prop risk manager (up to 120 traders), now runs a small prop firm in Spain; energy spread trader
markets: futures: WTI (NYMEX), Brent (ICE) calendar spreads, flies and condors; formerly Schatz, Bobl, Bund
edge_principles: Risk-manager 'traffic light' daily loss rule: at ~40% of the daily stop, warn and suggest smaller size; at ~60-70%, take a break, flatten and cut size until half is recovered; at 100%, done for the day.
Daily stops differ by trader, product and track record; proven traders who recover from drawdowns get wider stops.
You do not need a high win rate: nine 1-tick losses and one 10-tick win is profitable; keep losses smaller than winners.
Learn to enjoy small losses because they replace large ones; inability to accept losses is the main beginner mistake.
Watching many traders' live positions and P&L taught him patterns of what works (how far they ran winners, averaging, sizing) before he became profitable.
Spreads (long one contract month, short another) have much smaller ranges and deeper books than outrights, and multi-leg structures can be adjusted leg by leg when wrong.
The best traders he managed cared about the game, not the money; trading for money you need makes it harder.
Fat-finger spikes happen (e.g. an 800-tick Schatz spike); trades may be busted but positions taken in the chaos still need managing.
notes: Prop risk management and spread-trading overview. Setups are futures calendar spreads (not testable in MCF) and a historical order-book pattern (spoofing 'flipper') that is now illegal.
